name: Daria Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, and thank you. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. This is confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior property manager in the lettings team of a mid-size agency on the edge of the city, so I look after about sixty rented flats for landlords. Most of my day is emails and phone calls: a leak at number 12, a tenant who wants to leave early, a landlord who won't pay for a new oven. Twice a week I'm out doing inspections with a tablet, ticking boxes and taking photos of damp patches. I like fixing things for people, and I hate deposit disputes, because somebody always ends up hating me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio flat, which I'm proud of, but it eats almost half my pay. I've got maybe a week or two of savings, because my rent went up in the summer. I use AI sometimes to tidy up a stiff email to a landlord, but not much more. There aren't many lettings jobs round here, and most agencies have one or two people doing what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, no big change. Fine, but my problems don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, that the tools are useful for small things and people should stop panicking. That's my general line on most things, honestly, let's see what actually happens. I'm not the type to post big opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worry isn't AI, it's my rent and my pay. My studio went up by ninety a month in July, and my pay went up by nothing. If the agency loses a couple of big landlords, they'll cut a property manager, and I'm the junior one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a review in January, with a list of what I've taken on since I started. I'd use the email tool more, to finish earlier and do the property management certificate online in the evenings. And I'd stop the streaming services and meal kits until I've got a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, a bit. Like I'm treading water and the water's getting colder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the agency loses big landlords, they'd cut someone. Is that likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of our biggest landlords, with eleven flats, is selling up next year because of new rules on energy ratings. That's a chunk of the work I do. So it's not a crazy fear, it's just maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on that list for your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inspections on time for six months, two deposit disputes settled without going to the scheme, and I trained the new girl on the system. I'd write it all down because I'd go blank in the meeting otherwise. I'm better on paper than in the room.

say: AI tools are **useful** for small things, and people should stop **panicking**.
Let's see what **actually happens** before getting worked up.
think: My real worry is **rent and pay**, not AI.
If the agency loses big landlords, the **junior property manager** goes, and that's me.
do: Ask for a **pay review** in January with a written list of my work.
Do the **property management certificate** online in the evenings.
Cancel **streaming and meal kits** until I have a month saved.
S0.quote: One of our biggest landlords, with eleven flats, is selling up next year because of new rules on energy ratings.
fieldNote: Daria's pressure in this picture is a **rent rise** and a big landlord **leaving**, not AI.
She's practical and **prepared**, writing lists because she freezes in meetings.
Her centre outlook shows as a calm, **wait and see** public line.

steps.text: Ask for a January pay review with a written list of achievements
Do the property management certificate online in the evenings
Cancel streaming and meal kits until one month is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, emails and booking and checking. That's my whole desk, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people in lettings should get trained, not just replaced. I'd probably say it at our team meeting and to my friends from school who work in offices. I'd be fair about it, though, because some of it really would make the job better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job gets split in two. The emails, the contractor booking and the rent chasing go to software, and what's left is inspections and the awkward conversations. They'd need maybe half as many people like me, and one of the two of us in my team would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the agency picks a system, then learn it properly, because I've seen people waste time on tools that get dropped. I'd push to do more inspections, because that's the part a computer can't do from a desk. And I'd finish the certificate, so I could apply for block management jobs, which have more site visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. I can see which way to lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, the other property manager, has been there nine years and she's brilliant on the phone but hates computers. Carol might actually be the safer one, because landlords love her. That would be hard to watch either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for the agency to pick a system. Is waiting a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. But I don't have the money to pay for courses on tools that might be gone next year. I'd rather learn the right one well than five wrong ones badly.

say: Lettings staff should be **trained, not replaced**.
Some of this would genuinely make the **job better**, and I'd say so.
think: My job **splits in two**: desk work to software, inspections and hard talks to me.
My team would need **half as many** people, so one of us **goes**.
do: Learn the agency's **chosen system** properly once it's picked.
Push to take on more **inspections**, which can't be done from a desk.
Finish the certificate and apply for **block management** jobs.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, because I can see **which way** to lean.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn the right one well than five wrong ones badly.
fieldNote: Daria clearly separates her **desk tasks** from the **site visits** that last longer.
She waits for proof before learning tools, true to a **steady** temperament.
She thinks her colleague **Carol** might be safer thanks to landlord loyalty.

steps.text: Learn the agency's chosen AI system once it's picked
Ask to take on more property inspections each week
Apply for block management jobs after the certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. That's two lease renewals for most of my tenants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from government and companies, both, not just one blaming the other. I'd say it calmly at work, because panic doesn't help a team. Online I'd share sensible stuff, not the scary videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 a computer does my desk job better than me and doesn't get tired of angry landlords. The inspections might hang on until robots arrive around 2031, but nobody pays a full wage just for inspections. I think I lose most of my income within two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move out of the studio as soon as my lease ends and share a flat, which I hate the idea of but it halves my rent. I'd look at work that's hands-on and near buildings, like a trainee building surveyor or a site inspector for a housing company. And I'd ask my parents if I could keep a room at theirs as a backstop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent of seven hundred, food, phone, travel, and maybe two weeks saved. If I lose the job in 2028 and it takes three months to find something, I'm short two thousand pounds. That number would be in my head every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're proud of living alone. What would giving that up feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like going backwards. I worked hard for my own front door. But a front door's not worth being broke, and I'd rather choose to give up my studio than be forced.

say: We need a plan from **government and companies**, not each blaming the other.
I'd stay **calm** at work and share **sensible** posts, not scary videos.
think: By **2028** a computer does my desk job better than me.
Inspections alone till **2031** won't pay a full wage, so most of my **income** goes.
do: Give up the **studio** at lease end and **flat-share** to halve rent.
Apply for **trainee surveyor** or site inspector work for housing firms.
Ask my parents to keep a **room** for me as a backstop.
S2.quote: A front door's not worth being broke, and I'd rather choose to give up my studio than be forced.
fieldNote: Daria expects to lose **most of her income** by around 2028, with inspections lasting a little longer.
She can put an exact figure on the gap: about **£2,000** short.
Giving up her **own front door** is her biggest emotional cost.

steps.text: Move from the studio into a flat-share when the lease ends
Apply for trainee building surveyor jobs with housing firms
Ask my parents to keep a room as a backstop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more like something you can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to adjust if people start now, and I'd encourage the younger ones at work to look ahead. I'd keep it practical, like here's a course, here's a job that needs people. That's more me than big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job lasts until around 2031, then shrinks fast. The inspections and dealing with people face to face stretch a bit further, maybe to 2034. So I'd have three or four years of normal pay to get somewhere safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time surveying course in 2027, because a surveyor is out on site checking walls and roofs. I'd stay in property management while I study, because I need the wage and the experience counts. I'd save a bit each month, even if it's just forty pounds, so I'm not starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more steady. Like I've got a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a surveying course on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some firms pay for it if you join as a trainee, so I'd target those. If not, I'd do it in small chunks and keep my studio a bit longer. I'd rather go slowly than not at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does surveying feel safe to you in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, because robots come in 2034 in this picture. But I'd have built skills a landlord trusts, and that counts for something. I'm not looking for forever, just the next ten years.

say: There's **time to adjust** if people start now.
I'd point the younger staff to **courses and jobs**, not give speeches.
think: My desk job lasts to about **2031**, then shrinks fast.
Face-to-face work stretches to **2034**, giving me a few years of **normal pay**.
do: Stay in **property management** while I study, for the wage and experience.
Save **£40 a month** so I'm not starting from nothing.
feel: Still anxious but **steadier**, with a **path** ahead.
S3.quote: I'm not looking for forever, just the next ten years.
fieldNote: Five years lets Daria **train while earning**, which she couldn't in the fast picture.
She still expects to **lose the desk job**, so she stays anxious.
She targets firms that **pay for training**, a sign of careful money sense.

steps.text: Start a part-time surveying course in 2027
Stay in property management while studying
Save £40 a month towards the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and people should use it, without panicking. I'd probably be the one in the office making a list of courses. Ten years is a long time in lettings, so most people wouldn't even notice at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right, if I keep moving. I'd have time to finish the property management certificate, get some experience, then move into surveying or block management. The money stays tight, but tight isn't a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certificate this year and go for a senior property manager role in three or four years. I'd learn the AI tools once the agency settles on them, because that'll be expected. Around year five, I'd start surveying, so I'm on site before robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. A bit uneasy, because rent is rent, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two weeks of savings. Does ten years really feel okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings are the bit that doesn't feel okay. My work plan feels fine with ten years. But one bad month could still knock me over, any year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I'm too careful and should just go and be a surveyor now. My mum would say keep the job you've got. I'd do something in the middle, which is what I always do.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so use it **without panicking**.
I'd be the one in the office making a **list of courses**.
think: I'll be all right if I **keep moving** towards surveying or block management.
Money stays **tight**, but tight isn't a **disaster**.
do: Finish the **property management certificate** this year.
Go for **senior property manager** in three or four years.
Start **surveying** around year five, before robots in **2039**.
feel: Fairly okay and **sleeping**, but **uneasy** about rent.
S4.quote: My dad would say I'm too careful and should just go and be a surveyor now.
fieldNote: With a decade, Daria feels her **own job path** is safe enough.
Her worry shifts to **savings**, which stay thin in any picture.
She describes herself as **in the middle**, between her parents' advice.

steps.text: Finish the property management certificate this year
Learn the agency's AI tools once they settle on one
Start surveying training around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for someone with a week or two of savings and no trade. What would help is employers paying for trainee places in things like surveying, and some help with rent while you retrain. I don't need a handout, I need a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about tenants. Lots of my tenants are older or don't speak English well, and an app won't sort out their problems. Somebody still has to knock on their door.

headlineQuote: I don't need a handout, I need a bridge.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old **junior property manager** looking after about sixty rented flats.
She lives alone in a **studio** that takes nearly half her pay, with **little savings**.
She's practical and in the middle, waiting for **proof** before learning new tools.
In every picture she plans a move towards **surveying** or site work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for someone with **no savings** and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: Employer-paid **trainee places** in work like surveying.
Some **help with rent** while she retrains.
